segments.title: Opening: Fog and Chancery — The World's Machinery

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, unhurried reading of one of the great novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over this series we'll be moving through Dickens chapter by chapter — the fog, the law, the love, the death, and the extraordinary human comedy in between.
Today we begin at the beginning — with a world choked in fog, a court that devours lives, and a house whose very name is a provocation.
Joining me are three people I could not be more delighted to have around this table.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose great gift is making craft feel like discovery rather than technique.
She reads a sentence and sees the machinery behind it — and somehow makes you love the machinery.

Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — the person you want beside you when Dickens starts describing an institution, because James knows exactly what those institutions did to real people.
He also has a dry wit that I find frankly alarming.

And Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels as audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive — he reads Dickens the way Dickens intended: aloud, with relish, with full awareness of the comic timing built into every sentence.
Let's begin where Dickens begins — in the fog.
What strikes me immediately, every time I return to this novel, is that Dickens opens not with a character but with a condition.
The fog isn't atmospheric decoration — it is the novel's governing metaphor for the fog of the law, the fog of class, the fog of identity itself.
And then, almost as a counter-movement, he gives us Bleak House itself — which is, against all expectation, warm.
Esther's description of the house is one of the most precisely observed passages of domestic comfort in all of Victorian fiction.
And it culminates in a sentence that I think is one of the great closing sentences of any chapter.

"with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House"
That final clause — "just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment" — is a composer's touch, not just a writer's.
And notice what he does structurally with that sentence — it's a single, enormous periodic sentence, everything held in suspension until the very last three words: "Bleak House."
You don't get the subject until the end.
The whole sensation of arriving — the warmth, the light, the jingle of cutlery in a distant kitchen — all of it pours over you before you even know what you're being told about.
When I record a passage like that, you have to resist the urge to rush it.
The sentence is doing something to the reader's body — building a kind of physical welcome — and you have to let it.
The description of Ada's room — "all flowers—in chintz and paper, in velvet, in needlework" — that's not interior design, that's a person's character rendered as a room.
What's worth holding onto is that this warmth is not accidental — it's strategic.
Dickens is constructing a moral geography in which Bleak House — a name that should mean desolation — turns out to mean the precise opposite.
The real bleakness is out there, in the court, in the city.
And the shadow that falls over this warmth comes from somewhere much older — from the house's own past, from the Dedlock lineage and its attendant curses.
There is a passage I find genuinely chilling, set generations before the novel's action, concerning a crippled ancestral lady of the Dedlock family.

"I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!"
What's remarkable is that this is not supernatural machinery for its own sake — it is the past making a juridical claim on the present.
In a novel obsessed with inheritance and entailment, a curse is almost a legal document.
That is exactly right, and it connects to something I find fascinating about how power operates in this novel — and I don't just mean the Dedlocks.
There is a scene in Chapter Forty-One that I think is one of the most controlled pieces of dramatic writing Dickens ever produced.
Tulkinghorn — the lawyer, the keeper of secrets — stops Lady Dedlock from leaving the room with a single, almost whispered sentence.
"Lady Dedlock, have the goodness to stop and hear me, or before you reach the staircase I shall ring the alarm-bell and rouse the house."
The prose tells us he does not stir hand or foot, does not raise his voice — and yet this is absolute power.
The stillness is the threat.
It's a masterclass in what I'd call the rhetoric of minimum force.
The phrase "without himself stirring hand or foot or raising his voice" — Dickens is very deliberately showing you what Tulkinghorn does not do, which makes what he does say land like a blow.
When I've performed this scene, the temptation is always to give Tulkinghorn a sinister purr — but the more terrifying reading is flat, almost bored.
He doesn't need to perform menace.
And that is precisely how the Victorian legal establishment operated — not through visible coercion, but through the quiet, lethal management of information.
Tulkinghorn is not an aberration in this world.
He is the system made flesh — polite, patient, and utterly without mercy.
Fog, curses, and a lawyer who doesn't need to raise his voice — we are very much inside the world of Bleak House now.

In the next segment, we'll look more closely at how Dickens builds his two narrative voices — and what it means that he trusts one of them to a young woman who keeps insisting she's nobody very special.

segments.title: Richard's Slow Unraveling — Ambition and Ruin

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme where we take Dickens's great novel apart, chapter by chapter, to see exactly how it works and why it still matters.
I'm your host, and today we're in the thick of one of the novel's central tragedies: the slow, almost imperceptible unraveling of Richard Carstone.
Richard is young, charming, genuinely loveable — and constitutionally incapable of sustained effort.
Dickens plants the seeds of that ruin very early, and today we're examining exactly where and how.
Joining me are three guests who bring very different lenses to this material.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — always asking what each part is doing.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who can tell us what the world Richard is stumbling through actually looked like from the inside.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than anyone ought to admit — who hears Dickens as performance first, text second.
Let's begin with the moment the novel makes Richard's fate feel both hopeful and already doomed — the scene where he and Ada confide their love to Esther.
What strikes me immediately about that scene — Richard and Ada on either side of Esther, confiding their love — is that Dickens is doing something almost unfair to the reader.
He makes it genuinely charming and funny and warm, so you cannot help but love these two.
And then Esther — with that quiet, steely wisdom she hides behind all the self-deprecation — puts her finger on exactly what their love will require.

"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself — and then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake."
Constancy, fortitude, perseverance — Esther is essentially writing Richard Carstone's death warrant in the gentlest possible language.
Because those are precisely the three qualities the novel will spend the next several hundred pages demonstrating he does not possess.
That's exactly right, and what makes it so devastating as a craft choice is the narrative voice doing it.
Esther as narrator is famously — almost infuriatingly — reluctant to judge.
So when she calmly lists constancy and perseverance as the conditions of their happiness, it doesn't read as a warning — it reads as a benediction.
But because we're reading with hindsight — or even just with attention — those words land like a diagnosis.
And that double effect — the warmth and the dread simultaneously — is Dickens at his most technically sophisticated.
I want to pick up on the word 'duty,' which Esther also uses there, because it carries a very particular weight in mid-nineteenth-century England.
For a young man of Richard's class and period, without independent means, duty meant choosing a profession and committing to it absolutely.
There were very few safety nets and a great deal of social shame attached to those who drifted.
What Jarndyce understands, and what Richard refuses to understand, is that his easy charm will not protect him from that world.
And Jarndyce does try to tell him so, in one of the novel's most direct pieces of advice.
That passage where he counsels Richard on Providence and effort — James, you've written about paternalism in Dickens; what do you make of Jarndyce here?
Jarndyce is doing something more nuanced than straightforward paternalism, I think.
He's explicitly disavowing authority — 'I have no power over you whatever' — while simultaneously making the moral case with complete clarity.
And the advice itself is bracingly practical for a man of Jarndyce's philosophical temperament.
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner.
Constancy in love is a good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy in every kind of effort."
That phrase 'like the heathen waggoner' is pure Jarndyce — slightly archaic, slightly biblical, but hitting the point with precision.
The heathen waggoner prays for help and doesn't bother to put his shoulder to the wheel.
Richard will spend the whole novel praying — in his fashion — for the lawsuit to deliver him, without ever putting his shoulder to anything at all.
And notice the final clause of that speech — which is extraordinary.
Jarndyce says, in effect: if you believe success can be won by fits and starts — leave that delusion here.
"Or leave your cousin Ada here."
Just that. Three words — 'or leave Ada.' Full stop.
As a performer, when you reach that line, you have to trust it completely and do absolutely nothing with it.
It's Dickens understanding that the biggest moments need the least decoration.
And Richard does, of course, choose neither option offered — he neither reforms nor relinquishes Ada.
He clings to both, which is exactly what a character without constancy would do.
But I want to spend a moment on the tender scene just before — Jarndyce to Ada and Richard about changing their feelings.
There's a line there that I find almost unbearably generous in its humanity.

"If you DO change — if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl — don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
'Nothing monstrous or uncommon' — that's Jarndyce refusing the melodrama that Victorian fiction so often reaches for.
It makes him one of the most quietly radical characters in the novel.
That generosity makes what follows even more painful — because Dickens closes that whole sequence with a piece of narration that is formally extraordinary.
Esther watches Richard and Ada leave through a sunlit room — Oliver, I know you have feelings about this passage.
I have very strong feelings about this passage, yes — it's one of the finest things Dickens ever wrote, I think, in the register of quiet devastation.
We see Richard bent over Ada's hand, talking earnestly; she looks up at him and seems to see nothing else.
And then the passage does this:

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness.
So they passed away into the shadow and were gone.
It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
The sun was clouded over.
Dickens has already written their tragedy in a change of light.
He doesn't need another word.
What's technically remarkable about that is the tense structure — or rather the aspect.
'They went on lightly' — past simple, continuous, hopeful. Then 'they passed away into the shadow and were gone' — the same tense, but suddenly it reads as finality.
And then the impersonal construction: 'the room darkened.' Not 'the clouds covered the sun' — the room darkened. As though the house itself registers the loss.
It's the narrator's grief being displaced into the architecture.
Which is absolutely appropriate for a novel called Bleak House — the buildings absorb the suffering of the people inside them.

I want to bring in the question of vocation here, because the sunlit scene is beautiful, but what follows it — Richard's actual professional life — is where the novel gets almost clinical in its diagnosis.
Mrs. Badger's assessment of Richard's relationship to medicine is — and I say this as someone who has spent years reading institutional records — extraordinarily accurate.
She says he's languid about the profession, that he doesn't have 'that positive interest in it which makes it his vocation.'
And then she offers this contrast — which is really also a quiet introduction to another character entirely:

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
That is a portrait of genuine vocation — the willingness to accept 'very little money' and 'considerable disappointment' because the work itself matters.
Richard has no such anchor. He is entirely dependent on expectation — and the only expectation he nurses is Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
And there's something almost cruel about the way Dickens positions Woodcourt here — not as a rival in any dramatic sense, but as a moral mirror.
Woodcourt does the work. Richard talks about the work, tries the work briefly, and then moves on.
And Mrs. Badger delivers this verdict with the calm certainty of someone who has seen it many times before — which is its own kind of institutional knowledge.
She's seen the Richards of the world come through the surgery and drift away. She doesn't judge. She simply describes.
It's a wonderfully Dickensian technique — the minor character who tells you the truth about the major one with devastating brevity.
This is where I want to circle back to the Lady Dedlock passages — because there's a structural parallel at work that I find fascinating.
We've been talking about Richard as someone undone by his relationship to the future — always waiting for Jarndyce and Jarndyce to deliver him.
Lady Dedlock is trapped in the opposite problem — imprisoned by the past, by something already done that cannot be undone.
And Tulkinghorn — patient, watchful, absolutely immovable — is the mechanism by which that past will destroy her.
Dickens describes their relationship at Chesney Wold with this extraordinary precision:
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine.
Mr. Tulkinghorn is always the same speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home."
'Exhausted deity' and 'speechless repository' — those two phrases are doing the work of entire character studies.
And then the novel pivots to what lies beneath the social surface — all that watching, all that mutual suspicion, all that hidden knowledge.
'Speechless repository of noble confidences' is a phrase I return to whenever I'm trying to explain what solicitors were in Victorian England.
Tulkinghorn holds the secrets of the aristocracy — their debts, their marriages, their indiscretions — and his power is precisely his discretion.
But Dickens shows us that what Tulkinghorn actually wants is not money, not advancement — it's the knowledge itself.
And the novel captures that perfectly in the passage's final sentence — all that watching and suspicion, all that mutual preparation for unawares moments.
"What each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
'For the time' — that qualifying phrase is doing everything.
It tells us this standoff will not last. The hidden things will come out. They always do, in Dickens.

And that, I think, is the thread running through everything we've discussed today — whether it's Richard's deferral of effort or Lady Dedlock's concealment of the past, the novel is always insisting that hidden things have consequences.
They accumulate. They compound. They eventually destroy.
Richard cannot see what Jarndyce sees clearly, what Esther narrates with that aching quiet, what Mrs. Badger diagnoses with professional frankness.
And the sunlit room will darken, as it always does.

In our next segment, we'll turn to the other great institution haunting this novel — Chancery itself — and ask how Dickens makes a court of law feel like a living organism, slowly consuming everything around it.

segments.title: The Crossing of Lives — How Dickens Weaves

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We're looking today at one of the things Dickens does with singular genius — the way he weaves disparate lives into a single, trembling web.
The great architectural question of Bleak House is how a stationer in Holborn, a dead law-writer, a baronet's wife, and a lost young man in Chancery all belong to the same story.
Eleanor Hartley has been looking closely at the passages that show us Dickens the craftsman at work — and I think she has things to say about his narration that might surprise us.
Eleanor, let's begin with the dead man — Nemo — watched in the dark as the Harmonic Meeting ends.
This is one of the passages I return to again and again, because what Dickens does here is almost unbearably deft.
The chapter has been comic — the Harmonic Meeting, the boozy company, the jingling piano — and then it stops.
He gives us that single line: the piano is silent, the friends go to their pillows, and now there is only the body.
And then the narrator does something extraordinary — he imagines backward in time.
He conjures a mother holding an infant, and asks us to feel the impossibility of this dead man ever having been that child.
The prose builds toward a cry — and it arrives here.
"Where is she, while these ashes are above the ground!"
It's not a question — it has an exclamation mark — it is an accusation levelled at the world for letting this happen.
And notice that we don't know the answer — Dickens doesn't give us one yet.
We know, because we've read the novel, that the woman is Lady Dedlock — that this wreck of a man was her great love.
But a first reader doesn't know that, and Dickens is banking on it.
He plants the emotional charge here — the grief, the waste, the severed connection — before we even have the names to attach it to.
As a reader of these novels aloud, I find that the omniscient narrator in these moments is almost a theatrical device — a chorus figure, lamenting on behalf of the audience.
The words have to be spoken to land — they were written to be heard.
What strikes me, listening to Eleanor and Oliver, is that Dickens is doing something politically pointed here as well as poetically.
Nemo dies in a room above a chandler's shop in a named slum, watched by nobody who knows his name.
That is not tragedy in the classical sense — that is a social indictment dressed in the language of tragedy.
The beauty of the prose is doing a kind of work that an official report or a parliamentary speech cannot do — it makes you feel the individual behind the statistic.
And Dickens gives us the physical world of those statistics just a few chapters later, when Snagsby is taken into Tom-all-Alone's.
Eleanor, that passage is yours as well — and it reads almost like a descent into hell.
It literally is — Dickens uses the word 'infernal gulf,' and Snagsby feels as if he's going deeper down into it with every step.
What I love about this passage technically is the accumulation of negatives.
The street is described as undrained, unventilated — the language of things that should exist but don't.
And then there is this brilliant parenthetical — listen to how it lands.
"Deep in black mud and corrupt water — though the roads are dry elsewhere."
That parenthetical is doing extraordinary work — it is the voice of conscience, saying: this is not nature, this is a choice.
The rest of London is dry — Tom-all-Alone's is not, and someone is responsible.
Eleanor has put her finger on exactly what makes that passage historically significant as well as literary.
Tom-all-Alone's is not a fantasy — it is a composite of real places: the rookeries of St Giles, the courts off Drury Lane, the slums that cholera kept finding because the sewers didn't exist.
The novel was published in 1852 and 1853 — one year before the great cholera outbreak of 1854, which finally broke the resistance to the idea that contaminated water killed people.
Dickens, in other words, was writing about a crisis that was still happening — not describing history, but shouting at the present.
The passage also works because of Snagsby himself — this mild, bewildered little man who has lived in London all his life and cannot believe his senses.
Dickens is very clever to send a civilian in, rather than an investigator — Bucket is used to it, Snagsby is not.
And the full sentence Dickens gives us is almost overwhelming in its accumulation — let me try it.

"A villainous street, undrained, unventilated, deep in black mud and corrupt water — though the roads are dry elsewhere — and reeking with such smells and sights that he, who has lived in London all his life, can scarce believe his senses."
Read it aloud and you're breathless by the end — which is precisely the effect Dickens wanted.
From the fog of the slums to the fog of the courts — James, you've been wanting to talk about what the novel says, with extraordinary directness, about the law itself.
There is a passage in Chapter 39 that reads less like a novel and more like a pamphlet.
Dickens drops the mask entirely in that passage — and what's underneath is pure fury, delivered with a kind of lethal calm.
He gives us what reads like a legal principle — and it is devastating.
"The one great principle of the English law is to make business for itself."
And he doesn't stop there — he says this is the only principle consistently maintained through all the law's narrow turnings.
Everything else — justice, equity, remedy — these are incidental.
The Court of Chancery was, historically, a system that generated fees for lawyers over generations while estates were frozen and litigants died waiting.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce is not a satire of one exceptional case — it is a portrait of how the whole machine worked.
What strikes me about that passage as a piece of writing is the mock-reasonable tone.
Dickens says — let the public but once clearly perceive that the law's grand principle is to make business for itself at their expense, and surely they will cease to grumble.
'Surely they will cease to grumble' — the irony is so controlled it almost sounds sincere.
And that is a specifically Swiftian technique — presenting the monstrous as logical, forcing the reader to complete the outrage themselves.
And then you turn from that cold rage to Richard Carstone — which is where it becomes heartbreaking rather than merely outrageous.
Because Richard isn't an abstraction — he's a young man who knows something is wrong with himself and cannot stop it.
His confession to Esther is one of the most painfully self-aware speeches in the novel.
"I understand you, and I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow... constant to myself."
He knows the diagnosis — inconstancy — and he cannot fill the prescription.
That parenthetical — 'Somehow, I mean something that I can't very well express, but you'll make it out' — that is Dickens's genius for a character speaking at the edge of their own understanding.
And the speech literally trails off — he says 'and shouldn't be in debt, and —' and the sentence stops.
That dash is one of the saddest pieces of punctuation in all of Dickens.
Richard can't finish his own sentence — because the sentence, completed, would force him to confront what Chancery is doing to him.
And there is another figure in this web who cannot be left out — Tulkinghorn.
Because Dickens shows us the law not just as a system but as an individual wielding it — and Tulkinghorn is that individual made flesh.
His speech to Lady Dedlock is a masterclass in power exercised with perfect composure — he tells her what he has, and what it means.
"I would as soon have hoped to root up by means of my own strength and my own hands the oldest tree on this estate as to shake your hold upon Sir Leicester."
He is telling her: you were untouchable — and now you are not.
That is not justice speaking — that is power, enjoying itself.
What I notice in that speech is the hesitation Tulkinghorn admits to — 'even now, with this case, I hesitate.'
Which is more frightening than certainty — it means he is choosing, moment by moment, what to do with her.
She is not in the grip of the law yet — she is in the grip of this one man's deliberation.
That image of being in the grip of one man's deliberation — it connects everything we've been discussing.
Nemo, undone by obscurity; Snagsby, overwhelmed by the city he thought he knew; Richard, unravelled by a system he can't escape; Lady Dedlock, held by a secret in a lawyer's keeping.
Dickens's web holds all of them — and none of them knows the shape of the thing they're caught in.
We'll be back after the break to look at how the novel's two narrators — Esther and the omniscient voice — create that double vision.

segments.title: Jo, the Outcast — Dickens's Indictment of Society

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great sprawling masterpiece apart — chapter by chapter, voice by voice, injustice by injustice.
I'm your host, and today we're diving into one of the novel's most devastating threads: Jo, the crossing-sweeper — a child who exists, in Dickens's world, at the absolute bottom of everything.
And we'll be asking a harder question alongside it: how does Dickens indict not just poverty, but the institutions — legal, social, moral — that manufacture it?
To work through all of that, I have three extraordinary guests with me.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for the architecture of a sentence is, frankly, alarming in the best possible way.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what Chancery was, what it did to real people, and why it matters that Dickens was so furious about it.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps anyone alive — brings the performer's ear to every syllable.
Let's begin where Dickens begins — in the coroner's inquest in Chapter Eleven, where Jo is called to testify.
The inquest scene is one of those passages where Dickens does three completely different things at once — and makes it look effortless.
You get Mrs. Piper first — this magnificent comic avalanche of parentheses and neighbourhood gossip.
Listen to how Dickens sets her up — and I'm going to read this because the prose itself is the joke.
"Why, Mrs. Piper has a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell."
'Chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell' — that is a sentence that does its own satirical work before a single parenthesis arrives.
And then Dickens delivers on it spectacularly — the half-baptizing of Alexander James Piper, aged eighteen months and four days old, because of the sufferings in his gums.
It's sublime rubbish — and it serves a deadly serious purpose, because it keeps Jo off the stand.
That structural juxtaposition is everything, isn't it.
Dickens gives Mrs. Piper this enormous, baroque, parenthetical performance — all that verbal excess — and then he gives us Jo.
And Jo speaks in the most stripped, monosyllabic prose in the entire novel.
Dickens is working with rhythm and density as a moral instrument here.
The passage describing Jo's testimony is almost percussive in its brevity — every sentence a closed door.
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Six words. Then five. No verbs. No grammar of connection. Just absence.
Dickens is making the form perform the content — Jo has no language because he has been given nothing with which to build one.
And the legal detail here is exact — and brutal.
Jo is turned away from giving evidence at that inquest because he cannot demonstrate sufficient religious understanding to take an oath.

That was precisely how the law worked in mid-Victorian England — competency to testify was contingent on a capacity for Christian belief, which presupposed education, which presupposed social inclusion.
Jo has been denied all three. And so the law, in its perfect circularity, denies him voice.
What Dickens captures is the self-sealing logic of exclusion: you are kept ignorant, and then your ignorance is used to justify keeping you excluded.
And yet — and this is what breaks you — Jo still tries to tell the truth.
He can't say precisely what will happen to him after death if he lies to these gentlemen, but he believes it'll be something very bad and he'll deserve it — so he'll tell the truth.
Dickens spells out his moral universe in the simplest possible terms: knows a broom's a broom, and knows it's wicked to tell a lie.
"Knows a broom's a broom, and knows it's wicked to tell a lie."
That's his entire education — and it is, in its way, more morally coherent than anything the lawyers around him manage.
The irony is so quiet Dickens almost doesn't announce it.
The passage about Nemo and Jo is where I think Dickens moves from polemic into something much stranger and more devastating.
Because Nemo — this unknown, unnamed man — turns out to be the only human being who has ever spoken to Jo as a human being.
There's this extraordinary moment — Jo shivering in a doorway, the man turning back.
"Neither have I. Not one!" and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.
Two outcasts recognising each other across the void — and the recognition taking the form of a shared meal.
It's almost sacramental in its simplicity. Dickens is working very close to the bone here.
What strikes me about that passage is the question Nemo asks Jo — whether he ever wished to die.
Dickens describes them as 'strange questions' — but of course they aren't strange at all; they're the questions any person living under those conditions would be asked.
What is strange is that anyone is asking them of Jo at all.
The novel keeps returning to this: the scandal is not only material deprivation, but the deprivation of being seen.
And the man who sees him is himself nobody — Nemo, literally No One, dead in a rented room.
Dickens is quietly savage about what society produces and then discards — these men who have been hooted and pursued about the streets.
'Hooted and pursued about the streets' — I always stop at that phrase when I read it aloud.
"That graceless creature only knows that the dead man was sometimes hooted and pursued about the streets."
'Graceless creature' — that's the voice of respectable society dismissing Jo even as Dickens is making us love him.
The free indirect discourse does all the indicting — Dickens never raises his voice, and the effect is shattering.
So the cruelty isn't incidental — it's systemic.
Which brings us to Chapter Thirty-Nine and Mr. Vholes — and the question of how the law protects itself from ever having to change.
James, this is your territory — what is Dickens doing with Kenge's defence of Vholes?
It's one of the finest pieces of institutional satire in the English novel — and I say that as someone who has spent a career reading documents produced by people who sound exactly like Mr. Kenge.
The argument runs like this: yes, this law causes delay, expense, and vexation — the attorney concedes all three.
But the law cannot be reformed, because reform would destroy a class of practitioners — and Mr. Vholes is their representative man.
Kenge's speech moves with this horrible, gliding reasonableness.
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
Notice how the rhetorical register shifts — from the professional gentlemanly 'my dear sir' to this sudden apocalyptic image.
As though the real catastrophe would not be children like Jo dying on the streets, but Mr. Vholes losing his practice.
The parliamentary inquiry section is almost unbearably funny — and almost unbearably grim — simultaneously.
Dickens gives the question numbers — 'Question number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight hundred and sixty-nine' — and that number is the joke.
It's a precise, formal rendering of bureaucratic infinity — the system has asked so many questions it has lost count.
And after all those hundreds of thousands of questions, the inquiry is stopped dead — for ten years — by a single answer.
"Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man."
'Respectable' — that word is doing the work of a battering ram throughout this novel.
It is the system's self-defence mechanism: invoke respectability, and reform dies in its cradle.
And then in Chapter Sixty we see what Vholes's 'professional duty' actually looks like in operation — which is monstrous.

He tells Esther — without a flicker of warmth — that Richard's affairs are in a very bad way, the marriage was ill-advised, and he regards this as a professional duty to declare, though it cannot be charged to anyone.
It's devastating because he is, in a narrow sense, telling the truth — and yet every word is a form of predation.
The phrase that haunts me is this — and Dickens has him note it in his diary, which is 'producible at any time.'
"I HAVE carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over to any connexion of Mr. C.'s on any account."
'I will not smooth things over' — said by a man whose entire existence smooths over his clients' ruin with the language of diligence and duty.
It is a masterclass in how institutional language colonises conscience.
The diary detail is precise and chilling — and historically accurate.
Victorian solicitors did maintain diaries of client conversations precisely for self-protection — producible at any time, as Vholes says.
Dickens had personal experience of the law's paper machinery — he'd worked as a clerk in various legal offices as a young man.
What he understood, and what Vholes embodies, is that the law's paperwork is not incidental to its cruelty — it is the cruelty.
Jo has no paper. No certificate, no record, no identity that the state recognises.
Vholes is drowning in it — and Richard is being consumed by it.
That is the symmetry Dickens is drawing — the paperless and the paper-bound, destroyed by the same machine from opposite ends.
That symmetry runs through the architecture of the whole novel — the alternating narrators, the two plots converging on a single catastrophe.
What's remarkable about this chapter — and about the Jo passages in Chapter Eleven — is the tonal control.
Dickens can shift from comic grotesque — Mrs. Piper and her parentheses — to this searing moral simplicity, without the joints showing.
That transition — from the rambling testimony of a woman who says a great deal but tells you nothing, to 'No father, no mother, no friends' — is one of the most devastating page-turns in fiction.
James's image of Jo and Richard destroyed by the same machine from opposite ends is one I want to carry into the rest of the episode.
Because the question it raises is: does Bleak House offer any escape from that machine?
Or does Dickens — with his clear eyes and his magnificent fury — ultimately leave us in the fog?
We'll pick that up in our next segment.

segments.title: The Unveiling — Lady Dedlock's Secrets and Shame

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great sprawling masterpiece and opens it up, chapter by chapter, passage by passage.
I'm your host, and today we're deep in the shadow of Chesney Wold, where secrets move through the air like weather.
Our subject is Lady Dedlock — the revelation of her hidden past, the machinery of concealment, and the man who embodies secret-keeping as a profession and a philosophy.
With me today are three remarkable guides to this territory.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — with delight in every working part.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what Chancery was, what it cost, and who paid for it.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than any living person — who hears the prose the way Dickens intended: as performance.
Let's begin with Mr. Tulkinghorn — because before we can talk about Lady Dedlock's secret, we have to reckon with the man who holds it.
Tulkinghorn is one of the great creations in all of Dickens — and that is saying something, given the competition.
What makes him extraordinary is precisely what makes him unreadable.
He arrives at Chesney Wold — Dickens gives us this superb description of the approach — and I want to read it, because the prose is doing something quite astonishing.
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every limb. Every crease. The man is a filing cabinet with a hat on.
But then Dickens does something even more interesting — he raises the question of Tulkinghorn's interior life and refuses to answer it.
"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret."
He is, as Dickens puts it, his own client. He will never betray himself.
What thrills me about that passage is the conditional: "if it be a mask."
Dickens plants a genuine epistemological uncertainty right there in the description.
Is Tulkinghorn performing expressionlessness, or is he simply — expressionless? We never know. Dickens doesn't know. The novel doesn't decide.
And that undecidability is the source of his power — over Lady Dedlock, over the reader, over everyone in the room.
Then look at what happens when he actually delivers his message to Lady Dedlock — through Sir Leicester, who reads it with agonising slowness.
That scene is a masterclass in dramatic irony. Sir Leicester is oblivious. Lady Dedlock is electrified. And we are watching both simultaneously.
I want to linger on the legal texture of that message, because it matters enormously.
The affidavit Lady Dedlock glimpsed — the handwriting that undid her composure — is a document in a Chancery suit.
Chancery at this period was a court of equity that had become a byword for delay and expense — cases running decades, fortunes consumed in legal costs.
The document that exposes Lady Dedlock's past isn't a letter, or a confession — it's a piece of legal paperwork. The machinery of the law contains the secret.
And now hear Tulkinghorn's message as Sir Leicester finally reads it aloud.
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
Three words. "I have seen him." The whole edifice of Lady Dedlock's concealment begins to crack at that sentence.
That landing — "I have seen him" — is pure theatrical craft.
Sir Leicester reads with his eyeglass, dawdling, finding the wrong line first — Dickens gives us the comedy of the oblivious man before the sting.
And then the scene that follows — the confrontation between Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn in the presence of Sir Leicester — is written like a duel conducted in perfect stillness.
Dickens describes their exchange, and then steps back to ask what none of us can answer.
"Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares."
"What each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
"For the time." That phrase is doing quiet, dreadful work. The time is running out.
That passage is perhaps the finest example in the novel of the omniscient narrator's strategic retreat.
The narrator who normally sees everything suddenly announces that he cannot — or will not — tell us what each character knows.
And that withdrawal of knowledge is itself terrifying. We feel the opacity as a kind of menace.
Meanwhile, Sir Leicester — magnificently — looks at the fire. He embodies an entire aristocratic tradition of not looking too closely.
Dickens says he has "the general expression of the Dedlock on the staircase" — meaning the painted ancestor above him, the family type reproduced in flesh.
Sir Leicester is not merely oblivious — he is constitutionally incapable of imagining that his world could be touched by this.
He says — and this is important — that no association in Lady Dedlock's mind could possibly be traceable to "this poor wretch."
The class condescension is total. The idea that Lady Dedlock, a baronet's wife, could have any human connection to a copying clerk is simply inadmissible to him.
Which points to a structural irony running through the whole novel — the secret that could destroy Lady Dedlock is protected, partly, by the social hierarchy that makes it unthinkable.
Her rank is simultaneously her prison and her shield.
That tension — rank as both protection and trap — connects directly to what Esther learns about her own origins.
Because the secret doesn't only belong to Lady Dedlock. It was imposed, from the very beginning, as a condition of Esther's existence.
Eleanor, that passage in Chapter Seventeen — where Jarndyce finally tells Esther what he knows — what do you make of the language of secrecy there?
It is devastating — and the devastation is entirely in the syntax.
This is Esther's narrative, remember — so we're hearing it through her careful, reticent voice.
Jarndyce tells her what he was told by Mr. Kenge — that the lady, her aunt, would never disclose more than the bare minimum.
"That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
"For any human consideration." The absoluteness of it. No appeal possible. No mercy built in.
And the parenthetical — "he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution" — is almost admiring. The resolution is presented as a kind of terrible virtue.
And she uses an assumed name. That detail arrives quietly and lands like a stone.
The lady estranged from "all intercourse with the world" — the lady who says, of her own accord, that her name is not her real name.
She has already unmade herself. She exists, socially and legally, under a fiction.
When you contrast that figure with Lady Dedlock — impeccably, publicly named, titled, placed — the symmetry is extraordinary.
One sister disappears into anonymity. The other armours herself in title and position. Same secret. Different strategies.
The assumed name is not merely personal — it has legal and social weight.
To live under an assumed name in Victorian England was to place yourself outside the normal web of record, of parish register, of legal identity.
It is precisely the kind of erasure available to women — particularly women in disgrace — who had very few other legal instruments of self-protection.
Jarndyce ends his account with four words: "My dear, I have told you all."
There is extraordinary gentleness in that — but also a finality. This is the shape of the knowledge. There is no more to give.
What strikes me, pulling these passages together, is how completely the secret is architectured — built into documents, names, silences, postures.
Tulkinghorn carries it in his creases. Lady Dedlock performs it as composure. Esther's aunt disappears inside it. Sir Leicester simply looks at the fire.
And the novel's great question — which Dickens refuses to answer easily — is what happens when that architecture finally gives way.
In our next segment, we follow Esther deeper into a world where secrets have already begun to collapse — and the cost is written on the faces of those who love her.

segments.title: Laughter in the Darkness — Bleak House's Comic Relief

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's great novel apart sentence by sentence — and puts it back together again with fresh eyes.
I'm your host, and today we're exploring one of the novel's most remarkable qualities: its ability to hold comedy and catastrophe in the same breath.
With me are three exceptional readers of this novel, each bringing something quite different to the table.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who cares passionately about how prose is actually constructed — the architecture beneath the surface.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what Dickens was describing when he described the law — and why it matters that he described it so precisely.
And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than anyone alive — he hears Dickens the way Dickens may have heard himself.
Today's passages range from pure gothic horror — a man dying in squalor — to one of the most perfectly calibrated comic marriages in English fiction.
That tension between darkness and laughter is, I'd argue, the very engine of this novel.

Eleanor, let's start with you — because you've been thinking about Dickens's narrative architecture, and I think the Nemo passage in chapter ten is a place where that architecture becomes almost unbearably visible.
It's a passage that stops you cold — and what stops you is partly the technique, the sheer craft of how Dickens positions the reader.
We're given the scene through Tulkinghorn's perspective — through a lawyer's eyes, standing in a doorway — which already tells us something.
The law looks upon misery and registers it — but with that terrible professional coolness.
And then Dickens does something extraordinary with the candle.
He describes it as having guttered down until the wick has doubled over — and he calls what forms above it a tower of winding-sheet.
A winding-sheet is a burial shroud.
So before we've even looked at the man in the bed, the candle above him is already dressed for a funeral.
That is not accidental — that is a writer in total command of his imagery.
Eleanor is absolutely right about the candle, and what strikes me as a reader-aloud is that the whole passage is structured like a slow approach.
Dickens builds up the room — the patchwork, the ticking, the coarse sacking — before he lets you see the man fully.
He's directing your eye like a cinematographer — a word he couldn't have known, but would certainly have understood.
And then that final assault on the senses — and I do want to read this aloud, because it has to be heard.
"through the general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco, there comes into the lawyer's mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium"
It's synaesthetic — the smell becomes a taste — and you feel how the corruption of this room has entered the man of law himself.
Even Tulkinghorn cannot stand in that doorway and remain entirely untouched.
What I'd add is the specific social geography of this scene — which Dickens understood with a historian's precision, whether or not he thought of himself that way.
Nemo's room — the bare feet, the coarse sacking, the opium — is not exotic poverty for Dickens's readers.
This was the recognisable death of a man of the copying class — a law-writer — who has drunk and drugged himself to the edge of extinction.
Opium in this period was cheap, legal, and widely used among the working poor precisely because it numbed the pain of unremitting drudgery.
So when Oliver says the room has entered the lawyer — that bitter taste — Dickens is also making a class argument.
The law feeds on these lives, and in some sense it carries a trace of them in its mouth — whether it knows it or not.
James's point about the class argument makes me want to jump ahead to Richard — because Richard's deterioration is the novel's long, slow Chancery death played out in a young man's body.
And the speech Dickens gives him in chapter twenty-three is structurally extraordinary — it's almost a legal brief, the argument conducted in extended parallel clauses.
Richard has been so colonised by Chancery that even his self-defence is structured like a Chancery document.
Listen to how the hypothetical conditions stack up, one on another, before he reaches his confession.

"If you lived in an unfinished house, you couldn't settle down in it; if you were condemned to leave everything you undertook unfinished, you would find it hard to apply yourself to anything; and yet that's my unhappy case."
Two conditional propositions — perfectly reasonable, perfectly logical — and then the ground gives way beneath them.
The sentence enacts the very instability it's describing.
That Chancery colonisation — to use Eleanor's word, and it's the right word — is something I find genuinely chilling when I look at it against the historical record.
Suits in Chancery in Dickens's time could run for decades — sometimes longer than a human life.
The court wasn't merely slow — it had no reliable mechanism for reaching a conclusion.
What Richard describes — being born into an unfinished contention, unsettled before he knew the difference between a suit at law and a suit of clothes — is historically precise.

There were real families like the Carstones: heirs to contested estates who never lived to see resolution, who had no stable identity because their fortune — and therefore their place in the world — remained perpetually deferred.
The law did not merely fail these people — it unmade them.
I want to come in here, because James and Eleanor have been beautifully serious — and rightly so — but I think we need to talk about where the comedy fits in this novel.
Because Dickens does not give us unrelieved darkness — he gives us Mrs. Snagsby.
And I am never not delighted by Mrs. Snagsby.
Her husband is a mild, hen-pecked stationer — a man of no great consequence in the world — who finds himself tangentially connected to dark secrets he barely understands.
And Mrs. Snagsby's response to her suspicions is to become — in Dickens's perfect phrase — his shadow.
"And henceforth he begins, go where he will, to be attended by another shadow than his own, hardly less constant than his own, hardly less quiet than his own."
The triple repetition of 'hardly less' — that's pure comic rhetoric, building with each beat.
And then he lands it — bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh, shadow of his shadow — the marriage vow turned into a comic curse.
What you've put your finger on, Oliver, is that the comedy and the gothic are doing the same structural work.
Mrs. Snagsby is a shadow — but so is Nemo, described a few chapters earlier in exactly those spectral, hovering terms.
The language of haunting runs through the whole novel — in the deaths, in the marriages, in the courts of law.
Dickens uses the same imagery for comedy and tragedy because he understands they're expressions of the same human truth.
We are all haunted — by the law, by the past, by the people we love most.

I want to add one thing about Jarndyce in chapter thirteen — because Jarndyce is the figure who holds all of this together, who tries to stand against the corrosive effects of Chancery on those he loves.
His speech to Richard and Ada is one of the most quietly affecting passages in the novel — and it's essentially an admission of his own limitations as a guardian.
He contemplated their union — but always at a distance, hedged, qualified.
"I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here (don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear!) being in a mind to go through life together."
Afar off — twice — that gentle, rueful repetition.
It is the voice of a man who has learned to keep hope at a careful distance — because Chancery has taught him what happens when you hold it close.
James's reading of that passage moves me every time — because there's comedy in it too, in the best sense.
Don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear — that little parenthetical interruption is Dickens the comic entertainer breaking through Dickens the tragic architect.
It makes Jarndyce fully human — fallible, tender, slightly flustered — in the middle of a speech of great seriousness.
That is the Dickens trick — he never lets the solemnity calcify.
The Dickens trick — I think we should put that on the door.
Comedy that deepens tragedy; gothic imagery that powers satire; a marriage vow that becomes a curse — and somehow it all illuminates the same truth.
Eleanor, James, Oliver — thank you.
We'll be back shortly to press deeper into the novel's extraordinary narrative structure — and the question of who, exactly, is doing the telling.

segments.title: Redemption and Reckoning — Law, Love, and Consequence

utterances.text: We come now to our final movement — and it feels right to call it that, because these passages form something close to a requiem.
Law, love, and consequence — and the terrible cost of pride kept too long.
James, I want to begin with you — and with the passage that stops the novel cold.
Nemo, dead on his bed, with a coffin standing ready beside him.
What does Dickens achieve in that single, devastating image?
What he achieves is a kind of legal autopsy performed with a novelist's scalpel.
Nemo has lived forty-five years — and in the eyes of the law, the parish, the record-keeping machinery of Victorian England, he has left nothing.
Dickens reaches for the most extreme image of erasure he can find.
He says that Nemo lies there with — and I want to read this precisely —
"lies there with no more track behind him that any one can trace than a deserted infant."
A deserted infant — not a dead man, not a pauper, but an abandoned child at the very beginning of life.
The simile collapses a lifetime into nothing — and in doing so, indicts every institution that allowed it.
What strikes me about that sentence is its grammatical cruelty.
A life of forty-five years is held inside a subordinate clause — "whose path in life has lain through five and forty years" — and then simply cancelled.
The sentence structure itself performs the erasure.
And yet that same chapter pivots — because Jo is there, grieving, and Dickens addresses him directly.
He calls Jo a rejected witness — someone whose testimony the law will not accept.
But Dickens says he is not quite in outer darkness, and the reason given is extraordinary.
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
Jo's illiterate grief is more luminous than all the law's vocabulary combined.
"He wos wery good to me, he wos" — six words that break you completely.
The spelling is doing enormous work there — it's not mockery, it's tenderness rendered phonetically.
When I read that passage aloud, I've learned the only thing to do is trust the silence afterwards.
Don't rush past it, don't explain it — just let it sit.
Dickens understood that simplicity, wielded at the right moment, is the sharpest instrument in the box.
And from that low grief we move to a grief of quite a different register — a pride so absolute it becomes its own kind of death.
James, Jarndyce tells Esther about Lady Dedlock's sister — and the letter she wrote to Boythorn.
This passage is, for me, one of the most quietly devastating in the entire novel.
Jarndyce is recounting it to Esther — who, of course, is the secret child born from that very wound.
And the language of the letter he describes is almost juridical in its finality.
"she wrote him that from the date of that letter she died to him — as in literal truth she did."
"And that the resolution was exacted from her by her knowledge of his proud temper and his strained sense of honour, which were both her nature too."
"She made the sacrifice, she said, and would live in it and die in it. She did both."
She did both — Jarndyce just adds that, without flourish, and it lands like a verdict.
What's so historically precise here is that this is exactly how honour operated as a social mechanism — it could demand a human sacrifice, and name that sacrifice virtue.
The phrase "strained sense of honour" is extraordinary — strained, not strong.
It carries the idea that honour, pushed too far, distorts — becomes something rigid and self-destructive.
And then the phrase — "which were both her nature too" — implicates her completely.
She is not destroying herself to spare him — she is enacting her own deepest character in the act of self-erasure.
Which makes it both noble and terrible — and Dickens refuses to simplify it into one or the other.
What strikes me as a performer is the parenthetical — "as in literal truth she did."
It's Jarndyce interrupting himself — as if he can't bear to let even a rhetorical death-phrase pass uncorrected.
He insists on the literalness — she died, actually, socially, completely — and that scrupulousness is heartbreaking in its precision.
It's also a structural echo — Nemo erased himself from record, and she erased herself by an act of will.
Two forms of self-obliteration — one enforced by poverty and circumstance, one chosen out of pride.
Which brings us to our final passage — and it feels like the emotional culmination of everything we've been circling.
Mrs. Rouncewell, the housekeeper, pleading with Lady Dedlock to save her son George.
James — class, duty, and a servant's extraordinary courage.
This is Dickens at his most politically alert — and most emotionally generous simultaneously.
Mrs. Rouncewell knows exactly what she's doing — she is crossing every social boundary that Victorian deference demands.
And she names that boundary herself, with clear eyes.
"My Lady, you may have some proud or angry reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know;
if so, pray, oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been passed in this family which she dearly loves."
She does not pretend the hierarchy doesn't exist — she simply asks Lady Dedlock to choose, just this once, mercy over pride.
And the terrible irony, of course, is that Lady Dedlock cannot comply without destroying herself.
"Pray, oh, pray" — that repetition is not redundancy, it's escalation.
It's the voice breaking on the second invocation — which is exactly what it would do.
And Dickens plants that extraordinary aside: "the old housekeeper pleads with genuine simplicity."
Genuine simplicity — as opposed to the performed emotion that Lady Dedlock's world traffics in.
It's the same note we heard from Jo — artless, direct, devastating.
That's one of the great structural arguments of this novel — that the inarticulate feel more truly than the eloquent.
And look at how she frames Lady Dedlock's distance — not as cruelty, but as nature.
"You go your own way always without help" — she's not condemning her, she's explaining her.
And that act of imaginative sympathy — from servant to mistress, across all that distance — is itself a form of grace.
It mirrors what Jo offered the dead Nemo — an unconditional recognition of the other person's humanity.
Which suggests that Dickens sees grace not as a quality of the privileged — but of the overlooked.
That feels, to me, like the deepest thing Bleak House is doing — and perhaps the best note on which to close.
A novel of institutions and fog and interminable law — and yet its moral centre is Jo, Mrs. Rouncewell, a woman who chose to vanish rather than compromise another's honour.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan — three readers who have made this novel feel, I hope, both alive and urgent.
We'll be back with more from Bleak House — because the fog, as Dickens knew, never entirely lifts.

The furniture, old-fashioned rather than old, like the house, was as
pleasantly irregular. Ada’s sleeping-room was all flowers—in chintz
and paper, in velvet, in needlework, in the brocade of two stiff
courtly chairs which stood, each attended by a little page of a stool
for greater state, on either side of the fire-place. Our sitting-room
was green and had framed and glazed upon the walls numbers of
surprising and surprised birds, staring out of pictures at a real
trout in a case, as brown and shining as if it had been served with
gravy; at the death of Captain Cook; and at the whole process of
preparing tea in China, as depicted by Chinese artists. In my room
there were oval engravings of the months—ladies haymaking in short
waists and large hats tied under the chin, for June; smooth-legged
noblemen pointing with cocked-hats to village steeples, for October.
Half-length portraits in crayons abounded all through the house, but
were so dispersed that I found the brother of a youthful officer of
mine in the china-closet and the grey old age of my pretty young
bride, with a flower in her bodice, in the breakfast-room. As
substitutes, I had four angels, of Queen Anne’s reign, taking a
complacent gentleman to heaven, in festoons, with some difficulty;
and a composition in needlework representing fruit, a kettle, and an
alphabet. All the movables, from the wardrobes to the chairs and
tables, hangings, glasses, even to the pincushions and scent-bottles
on the dressing-tables, displayed the same quaint variety. They
agreed in nothing but their perfect neatness, their display of the
whitest linen, and their storing-up, wheresoever the existence of a
drawer, small or large, rendered it possible, of quantities of
rose-leaves and sweet lavender. Such, with its illuminated windows,
softened here and there by shadows of curtains, shining out upon the
starlight night; with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its
hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with
the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and
just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything
we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House.

“She had been a lady of a handsome figure and a noble carriage. She
never complained of the change; she never spoke to any one of being
crippled or of being in pain, but day by day she tried to walk upon
the terrace, and with the help of the stone balustrade, went up and
down, up and down, up and down, in sun and shadow, with greater
difficulty every day. At last, one afternoon her husband (to whom she
had never, on any persuasion, opened her lips since that night),
standing at the great south window, saw her drop upon the pavement.
He hastened down to raise her, but she repulsed him as he bent over
her, and looking at him fixedly and coldly, said, ‘I will die here
where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I
will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when
calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen
for my step!’”
c7:p59.summary: The crippled lady, after her husband finds her on the pavement, looks at him coldly and curses the Dedlock family: she will walk the terrace forever as a warning of coming calamity and disgrace.

alarm-bell and rouse the house. And then I must speak out before

Jo, is it thou? Well, well! Though a rejected witness, who “can’t
exactly say” what will be done to him in greater hands than men’s,
thou art not quite in outer darkness. There is something like a
distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: “He wos wery
good to me, he wos!”
c11:p100.summary: The narrator directly addresses Jo, acknowledging his legal rejection but affirming that his love for the dead man is a form of grace and light.

c43:p123.text:
“It was her act, and she kept its motives in her inflexible heart. He
afterwards did conjecture (but it was mere conjecture) that some
injury which her haughty spirit had received in her cause of quarrel
with her sister had wounded her beyond all reason, but she wrote him
that from the date of that letter she died to him—as in literal
truth she did—and that the resolution was exacted from her by her
knowledge of his proud temper and his strained sense of honour, which
were both her nature too. In consideration for those master points in
him, and even in consideration for them in herself, she made the
sacrifice, she said, and would live in it and die in it. She did
both, I fear; certainly he never saw her, never heard of her from
that hour. Nor did any one.”

c55:p71.text:
“Hush! Hush!” The housekeeper looks round and answers in a frightened
whisper, “My Lady, I have not breathed a word of it, I don’t believe
what’s written in it, I know it can’t be true, I am sure and certain
that it is not true. But my son is in danger, and you must have a
heart to pity me. If you know of anything that is not known to
others, if you have any suspicion, if you have any clue at all, and
any reason for keeping it in your own breast, oh, my dear Lady, think
of me, and conquer that reason, and let it be known! This is the most
I consider possible. I know you are not a hard lady, but you go your
own way always without help, and you are not familiar with your
friends; and all who admire you—and all do—as a beautiful and
elegant lady, know you to be one far away from themselves who can’t
be approached close. My Lady, you may have some proud or angry
reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray,
oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been
passed in this family which she dearly loves, and relent, and help to
clear my son! My Lady, my good Lady,” the old housekeeper pleads with
genuine simplicity, “I am so humble in my place and you are by nature
so high and distant that you may not think what I feel for my child,
but I feel so much that I have come here to make so bold as to beg
and pray you not to be scornful of us if you can do us any right or
justice at this fearful time!”
